Heart Disease Prediction using Machine Learning¶

Course: CSE-4115 Machine Learning  |  Department of CSE, BAUET

Student ID: 0812310205101023

1. Project Overview¶

Cardiovascular disease is one of the leading causes of death worldwide. Machine learning models that estimate a patient's risk from routine clinical measurements can support early diagnosis and help clinicians prioritise further tests.

This project builds and compares supervised binary classification models that predict whether a patient has heart disease (HeartDisease = 1) or not (HeartDisease = 0) from 11 clinical features.

Dataset: Heart Failure Prediction Dataset — fedesoriano (Kaggle)
A copy is included in this repository at data/heart.csv (918 patients, 12 columns). The dataset combines five well-known heart-disease databases (Cleveland, Hungarian, Switzerland, Long Beach VA and Statlog).

Target variable: HeartDisease (1 = heart disease present, 0 = no heart disease)

Workflow followed:

  1. Load and inspect the data
  2. Handle invalid/missing values and encode categorical variables
  3. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) with histograms, heatmaps and pair plots
  4. Split into training and testing sets and scale the features
  5. Train six classifiers (Logistic Regression, KNN, Gaussian Naive Bayes, Decision Tree, Random Forest, SVM)
  6. Evaluate with accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, confusion matrix and ROC-AUC
  7. Improve the models with 5-fold cross-validation and GridSearchCV
  8. Identify the most important clinical features
  9. Summarise findings, limitations and future work

A fixed random seed (RANDOM_STATE = 42) makes every split, model and plot reproducible.

Observations

  • The dataset has 918 patients and 12 columns (11 features + target), with no NaN values and no duplicate rows.
  • The target is fairly balanced: 553 patients (55.3%) have heart disease and 410 (44.7%) do not. Accuracy is therefore meaningful, but we still report precision, recall and F1.
  • RestingBP and Cholesterol are recorded as integers, but physiologically impossible zero values appear: 172 patients have Cholesterol = 0 and 1 patient has RestingBP = 0. These are effectively missing measurements, not real zeros, so we treat them as missing.
  • Categorical variables: Sex (M/F), ChestPainType (ATA/NAP/ASY/TA), RestingECG (Normal/ST/LVH), ExerciseAngina (Y/N) and ST_Slope (Up/Flat/Down). FastingBS is binary (0/1).

4. Data Cleaning and Preprocessing¶

Step Treatment Reason
Invalid zeros Replace Cholesterol = 0 and RestingBP = 0 with NaN A cholesterol or blood-pressure value of zero is not physiologically possible
Missing values Median imputation inside the modelling pipeline Robust to outliers and fitted only on the training data
Categorical variables One-hot encoding (drop="first") Models require numeric input; dropping one level avoids perfect collinearity
Numeric variables StandardScaler Required for distance-based (KNN, SVM) and regularised (Logistic Regression) models
Leakage control All imputation/encoding/scaling inside a Pipeline The test set is never used to fit preprocessing parameters

We first inspect the invalid values, then replace them with NaN so the pipeline can impute them.

In [3]:
df = df_raw.copy()

invalid_zero_counts = {
    "Cholesterol": int((df["Cholesterol"] == 0).sum()),
    "RestingBP": int((df["RestingBP"] == 0).sum()),
}
print("Physiologically impossible zeros:", invalid_zero_counts)

# Treat impossible zeros as missing measurements
df["Cholesterol"] = df["Cholesterol"].replace(0, np.nan)
df["RestingBP"] = df["RestingBP"].replace(0, np.nan)

print("\nMissing values after marking invalid zeros as NaN:")
print(df.isna().sum()[df.isna().sum() > 0].to_string())

print("\nZeros by target class (data-quality check):")
display(pd.crosstab(df["HeartDisease"], df["Cholesterol"].isna(),
                    rownames=["HeartDisease"], colnames=["Cholesterol missing"]))

Physiologically impossible zeros: {'Cholesterol': 172, 'RestingBP': 1}

Missing values after marking invalid zeros as NaN:
RestingBP        1
Cholesterol    172

Zeros by target class (data-quality check):
Cholesterol missing False True
HeartDisease
0 390 20
1 356 152

Important data-quality insight. Of the 172 zero-cholesterol records, 152 belong to patients with heart disease. If the zeros are left as real values, the average cholesterol of the disease group is artificially pulled down and the feature even appears negatively correlated with heart disease. After marking them as missing, the misleading pattern disappears (the correlation becomes weakly positive, ≈ +0.10). This shows why domain knowledge must precede purely automatic preprocessing.

Insight. The classes are close to balanced (55.3% disease vs 44.7% no disease), so a model cannot gain much by always predicting the majority class. Accuracy is a fair headline metric here, but recall (catching actual patients) is especially important in a screening context, because a missed diagnosis is more costly than a false alarm.

                Age  RestingBP  Cholesterol   MaxHR  Oldpeak
HeartDisease                                                
0             50.55     130.18       238.68  148.15     0.41

Insights.

  • Age: patients with heart disease are older on average (≈ 55.9 vs 50.6 years). The disease rate rises steadily from about 36% in the 30–40 group to about 74% in the 60–70 group.
  • Maximum heart rate (MaxHR): disease patients reach a much lower maximum heart rate (≈ 128 vs 148 bpm). A lower achievable heart rate under stress is a recognised risk indicator.
  • Oldpeak: the ST-depression value is clearly shifted upwards for disease patients (≈ 1.27 vs 0.41). Rates rise from about 35% for Oldpeak ≤ 0 to over 90% for Oldpeak > 2.
  • Cholesterol: after treating impossible zeros as missing, the distributions are similar and cholesterol is only weakly associated with the outcome. The raw data would misleadingly suggest a negative relationship because most zero records belong to the disease group.
  • Resting blood pressure: only a slight shift; it is a weak single predictor in this sample.

Insights.

  • Sex: men have a much higher disease rate (63.2%) than women (25.9%).
  • Chest pain type: ASY (asymptomatic) is associated with the highest rate (79.0%), while ATA (atypical angina) has the lowest (13.9%). This counter-intuitive pattern is well known in this dataset: many patients with silent ischemia are labelled ASY, and ATA often corresponds to a less severe presentation.
  • Exercise-induced angina: patients who experience angina during exercise have an 85.2% disease rate versus 35.1% for those who do not.
  • ST slope: a flat (82.8%) or down-sloping (77.8%) ST segment is far more associated with disease than an up-sloping segment (19.7%).
  • Fasting blood sugar > 120 mg/dl: disease rate 79.4% vs 48.0%, a meaningful signal (and a known diabetes-related risk factor).
  • Resting ECG: differences are modest (51.6%–65.7%); this feature is the weakest of the categorical variables.

6. Train/Test Split and Preprocessing Pipeline¶

We use an 80/20 stratified split, so both sets preserve the 55/45 class balance. All imputation, one-hot encoding and standardisation happen inside a scikit-learn Pipeline fitted on the training data only.

In [12]:
X = df.drop(columns=["HeartDisease"])
y = df["HeartDisease"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.20, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, stratify=y
)

print(f"Training set: {X_train.shape[0]} rows x {X_train.shape[1]} columns")
print(f"Test set    : {X_test.shape[0]} rows x {X_test.shape[1]} columns")
print(f"Disease rate - train: {y_train.mean():.3f} | test: {y_test.mean():.3f}")

numeric_features = ["Age", "RestingBP", "Cholesterol", "FastingBS", "MaxHR", "Oldpeak"]
categorical_features = ["Sex", "ChestPainType", "RestingECG", "ExerciseAngina", "ST_Slope"]

numeric_transformer = Pipeline(steps=[
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
])
categorical_transformer = Pipeline(steps=[
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", drop="first", sparse_output=False)),
])

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[
        ("num", numeric_transformer, numeric_features),
        ("cat", categorical_transformer, categorical_features),
    ],
    verbose_feature_names_out=False,
)

preview = preprocessor.fit_transform(X_train)
feature_names = preprocessor.get_feature_names_out()
print(f"\nTransformed training matrix: {preview.shape[0]} rows x {preview.shape[1]} features")
print("Encoded feature names:")
print(list(feature_names))

Training set: 734 rows x 11 columns
Test set    : 184 rows x 11 columns
Disease rate - train: 0.553 | test: 0.554

Transformed training matrix: 734 rows x 15 features
Encoded feature names:
['Age', 'RestingBP', 'Cholesterol', 'FastingBS', 'MaxHR', 'Oldpeak', 'Sex_M', 'ChestPainType_ATA', 'ChestPainType_NAP', 'ChestPainType_TA', 'RestingECG_Normal', 'RestingECG_ST', 'ExerciseAngina_Y', 'ST_Slope_Flat', 'ST_Slope_Up']

The transformed matrix has 15 columns: six scaled numeric features and nine one-hot columns (the first level of each categorical variable is dropped). The imputer is essential because Cholesterol contains 172 missing values after the invalid zeros are removed. Because the transformer is cloned inside each model pipeline, its parameters are re-estimated on every cross-validation fold and grid-search candidate.

7. Model Building and Evaluation¶

We train six classifiers, covering the model families taught in the course:

  1. Logistic Regression — linear probabilistic baseline (Lec-05)
  2. K-Nearest Neighbors — distance-based instance learner (Lec-07)
  3. Gaussian Naive Bayes — probabilistic Bayes classifier (Lec-06)
  4. Decision Tree — rule-based non-linear model (Lec-08)
  5. Random Forest — bagged ensemble of trees (Lec-11)
  6. Support Vector Machine (RBF) — maximum-margin classifier (Lec-09, optional extension)

Metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, confusion matrix and ROC-AUC for the positive class (heart disease = 1).

In [13]:
def build_pipeline(estimator):
    # Return an unfitted preprocessing + model pipeline
    return Pipeline(steps=[
        ("preprocess", clone(preprocessor)),
        ("model", estimator),
    ])


def compute_metrics(y_true, y_pred, y_proba):
    return {
        "Accuracy": accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred),
        "Precision": precision_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0),
        "Recall": recall_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0),
        "F1-score": f1_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0),
        "ROC-AUC": roc_auc_score(y_true, y_proba),
    }


models = {
    "Logistic Regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "K-Nearest Neighbors": KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5),
    "Gaussian Naive Bayes": GaussianNB(),
    "Decision Tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "Random Forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1),
    "Support Vector Machine": SVC(kernel="rbf", probability=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
}

fitted_models = {}
predictions = {}
probabilities = {}
results = {}

for name, estimator in models.items():
    pipeline = build_pipeline(estimator)
    pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)

    y_pred = pipeline.predict(X_test)
    y_proba = pipeline.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

    fitted_models[name] = pipeline
    predictions[name] = y_pred
    probabilities[name] = y_proba
    results[name] = compute_metrics(y_test, y_pred, y_proba)

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results).T.sort_values("Accuracy", ascending=False)
results_df.round(4)

7.4 ROC curves¶

ROC-AUC measures how well a model ranks patients by risk across all possible thresholds.

In [17]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
for name in fitted_models:
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, probabilities[name])
    auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, probabilities[name])
    ax.plot(fpr, tpr, linewidth=2, label=f"{name} (AUC = {auc:.3f})")

ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", linewidth=1, label="Random guess")
ax.set_xlabel("False positive rate")
ax.set_ylabel("True positive rate")
ax.set_title("ROC curves — test set")
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(FIG_DIR / "09_roc_curves.png", bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

Initial results discussion. (Test set: 184 patients.)

  • Logistic Regression is the strongest model on this test split: accuracy 0.8859, precision 0.8857, recall 0.9118, F1 0.8986 and ROC-AUC 0.9323. The clinical features are already close to linearly separable after scaling and one-hot encoding, and L2 regularisation keeps the model stable.
  • Gaussian Naive Bayes is a surprisingly strong second (accuracy 0.8750, F1 0.8844) and actually has the highest ROC-AUC (0.9430). Its independence assumption is violated, but the per-feature class distributions still rank patients well. Its cross-validation score is lower (Section 8), so this single split flatters it.
  • SVM (accuracy 0.8696, F1 0.8846, AUC 0.9360) and Random Forest (0.8641, F1 0.8768) are close behind. SVM's recall (0.9020) is between Logistic Regression's (0.9118) and Gaussian Naive Bayes's (0.8627), which matters for screening.
  • KNN is competitive but slightly weaker (accuracy 0.8478, F1 0.8627); distance-based methods suffer in a 15-dimensional space and are sensitive to the choice of k.
  • Decision Tree is the clear outlier (0.7391 accuracy, F1 0.7624). An unpruned tree memorises the training data and generalises poorly, which is exactly the variance problem that Random Forest is designed to reduce.
  • With only 184 test patients, a difference of two or three patients changes accuracy by about 1–1.5 percentage points, so small gaps between the top five models should not be over-interpreted. This is why the next section adds cross-validation.

8. Cross-Validation¶

A single split can be lucky or unlucky, so we run 5-fold stratified cross-validation on the training set for every model. Preprocessing is re-fitted inside each fold. We report mean and standard deviation of accuracy and F1.

In [18]:
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
scoring = ["accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1"]

cv_rows = {}
cv_fold_scores = {}

for name, estimator in models.items():
    pipeline = build_pipeline(estimator)
    scores = cross_validate(pipeline, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring=scoring, n_jobs=-1)
    cv_rows[name] = {
        "CV Accuracy": scores["test_accuracy"].mean(),
        "CV Accuracy Std": scores["test_accuracy"].std(),
        "CV Precision": scores["test_precision"].mean(),
        "CV Recall": scores["test_recall"].mean(),
        "CV F1": scores["test_f1"].mean(),
        "CV F1 Std": scores["test_f1"].std(),
    }
    cv_fold_scores[name] = scores["test_accuracy"]

cv_df = pd.DataFrame(cv_rows).T.sort_values("CV Accuracy", ascending=False)
display(cv_df.round(4).style.background_gradient(cmap="Greens", subset=["CV Accuracy", "CV F1", "CV Recall"]))
cv_df.to_csv(REPORT_DIR / "cross_validation.csv")

Cross-validation insights. (5-fold stratified CV on the 734 training patients.)

  • SVM has the highest mean CV accuracy (0.8584), followed by Random Forest (0.8529) and Logistic Regression (0.8515). The ordering is different from the single test split, where Logistic Regression came first — a useful reminder that a 184-patient test set is noisy.
  • On mean CV F1, the order is again SVM (0.8768), Random Forest (0.8708), Logistic Regression (0.8671), KNN (0.8616), Gaussian Naive Bayes (0.8552) and Decision Tree (0.8123).
  • Fold-to-fold standard deviations are 0.03–0.05 for accuracy, so the top three models are statistically very close; SVM's 0.007 lead over Random Forest is well within one standard deviation.
  • Logistic Regression is the most stable of the top group (accuracy std 0.029), while SVM has the largest spread (0.046).
  • Decision Tree is consistently the weakest (CV accuracy 0.7915), confirming that a single unpruned tree overfits.
  • Random Forest has a strong CV F1 and a clear non-linear mechanism, so it is a sensible candidate for hyperparameter tuning alongside Logistic Regression.

9. Hyperparameter Tuning with GridSearchCV¶

9.1 Random Forest¶

We search:

  • n_estimators — number of trees (100, 200, 300)
  • max_depth — maximum tree depth (4, 6, 8, unlimited)
  • min_samples_split — minimum samples to split a node (2, 5)
  • min_samples_leaf — minimum samples at a leaf (1, 2)

That is 48 combinations × 5 folds = 240 fits. The refit metric is F1-score, which balances precision and recall and is appropriate for a screening task where false negatives matter.

In [20]:
rf_param_grid = {
    "model__n_estimators": [100, 200, 300],
    "model__max_depth": [4, 6, 8, None],
    "model__min_samples_split": [2, 5],
    "model__min_samples_leaf": [1, 2],
}

rf_grid = GridSearchCV(
    estimator=build_pipeline(RandomForestClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1)),
    param_grid=rf_param_grid,
    cv=cv,
    scoring="f1",
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbose=1,
)
rf_grid.fit(X_train, y_train)

print("\nBest parameters:")
for key, value in rf_grid.best_params_.items():
    print(f"  {key.replace('model__', '')}: {value}")
print(f"\nBest cross-validated F1: {rf_grid.best_score_:.4f}")

rf_tuned = rf_grid.best_estimator_
rf_tuned_pred = rf_tuned.predict(X_test)
rf_tuned_proba = rf_tuned.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
rf_tuned_metrics = compute_metrics(y_test, rf_tuned_pred, rf_tuned_proba)

9.2 Logistic Regression¶

We tune the inverse regularisation strength C; smaller values mean stronger L2 regularisation.

In [22]:
lr_param_grid = {"model__C": [0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0]}

lr_grid = GridSearchCV(
    estimator=build_pipeline(LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)),
    param_grid=lr_param_grid,
    cv=cv,
    scoring="f1",
    n_jobs=-1,
)
lr_grid.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f"Best C: {lr_grid.best_params_['model__C']}")
print(f"Best cross-validated F1: {lr_grid.best_score_:.4f}")

lr_tuned = lr_grid.best_estimator_
lr_tuned_pred = lr_tuned.predict(X_test)
lr_tuned_proba = lr_tuned.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
lr_tuned_metrics = compute_metrics(y_test, lr_tuned_pred, lr_tuned_proba)

comparison_lr = pd.DataFrame({
    "Logistic Regression (default)": results_df.loc["Logistic Regression"],
    "Logistic Regression (tuned)": pd.Series(lr_tuned_metrics),
}).T[["Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "F1-score", "ROC-AUC"]]
display(comparison_lr.round(4).style.background_gradient(cmap="Purples", axis=0))
comparison_lr.to_csv(REPORT_DIR / "tuning_logistic_regression.csv")

9.3 Effect of tuning¶

The tuned Random Forest selects max_depth = 8, min_samples_leaf = 1, min_samples_split = 2 and n_estimators = 100. Its cross-validated F1 improves from 0.8708 to 0.8766 (+0.0058), which is the criterion used to select it. On the single held-out test set, however, accuracy moves from 0.8641 to 0.8587 and F1 from 0.8768 to 0.8725 — a small decrease that is well within the fold-to-fold noise seen in Section 8.

For Logistic Regression, the best C = 0.1 improves CV F1 from 0.8671 to 0.8685 (+0.0014), but its test accuracy falls from 0.8859 to 0.8696 (F1 0.8986 → 0.8824), while test ROC-AUC rises slightly (0.9323 → 0.9346).

Interpretation. Hyperparameter tuning did what it is supposed to do — it improved the cross-validated F1 on the training data — but the 184-patient test split is too small for that small improvement to show up reliably. We keep the default Logistic Regression as the best test-split model and report the tuned models transparently; we do not select hyperparameters by test-set performance, because that would leak information. The tuned models are included in the final ranking below for completeness.

10. Feature Importance and Model Interpretation¶

We use three complementary methods:

  1. Impurity-based importance from the tuned Random Forest.
  2. Permutation importance on the test set (model-agnostic, measures the accuracy drop when a feature is shuffled).
  3. Standardised coefficients from the tuned Logistic Regression (direction and strength of the effect on the log-odds of heart disease).

Feature-importance interpretation.

  • ST slope is the dominant feature by impurity importance: ST_Slope_Up (0.203) and ST_Slope_Flat (0.126). An up-sloping ST segment is protective, while flat or down-sloping segments sharply increase predicted risk. Permutation importance agrees strongly (ST_Slope = 0.150 mean accuracy drop, more than four times the next feature).
  • MaxHR (0.107) and Oldpeak (0.106) are the next most important in the Random Forest. A high achievable maximum heart rate is protective; greater ST depression (Oldpeak) is harmful. Both are direct markers of exercise-related cardiac ischemia.
  • Sex is the second strongest feature under permutation importance (0.034) even though its impurity score is smaller (0.036), because the forest can partly encode sex through correlated features. Being male increases risk substantially.
  • Chest pain type (ChestPainType_ASY) and exercise-induced angina (ExerciseAngina_Y) follow; both are clinically meaningful. FastingBS, Cholesterol and Age contribute smaller but non-zero amounts. Cholesterol is weaker here after the impossible zeros are corrected.
  • RestingECG has low importance in both rankings, matching its small univariate differences.
  • The impurity and permutation rankings broadly agree on the top features (ST slope, MaxHR/Oldpeak, Sex, chest pain, exercise angina), which gives confidence that these features genuinely improve held-out accuracy rather than merely fitting the trees.
  • The logistic coefficients confirm the directions: ST_Slope_Flat, Sex_M, ExerciseAngina_Y, FastingBS and Oldpeak are positive; MaxHR, ST_Slope_Up and the non-ASY chest-pain types (ATA, NAP, TA) are negative. ASY and Down are the dropped reference levels, so they appear as the baseline rather than as separate coefficients.

13. Conclusion¶

This project applied a complete supervised machine-learning workflow to heart-disease prediction.

Main findings

  1. Strong, clinically meaningful signal. The best model (Logistic Regression) reaches 88.6% accuracy, 0.899 F1-score, 0.912 recall and 0.932 ROC-AUC on the held-out test set — far above the 55.3% majority-class baseline. Cross-validation gives a slightly more conservative accuracy estimate of about 85–86%, which is the more trustworthy figure.
  2. The strongest predictors are exercise-related cardiac measurements. ST_Slope dominates all importance rankings, followed by Oldpeak, MaxHR, ExerciseAngina, ChestPainType and Sex. This agrees with clinical knowledge: ST-segment behaviour and exercise response are central to ischemia assessment.
  3. Sex and age matter. Men have a much higher disease rate than women (63.2% vs 25.9%), and the disease rate rises from about 36% (ages 30–40) to about 74% (ages 60–70).
  4. Data quality changed the story. Treating the 172 impossible zero cholesterol values as missing revealed that cholesterol's apparent negative association was an artefact; after cleaning, its correlation is only weakly positive (≈ +0.10). Domain-aware preprocessing was essential and is one of the most important lessons of the project.
  5. Simple models are competitive. Logistic Regression gives the best test accuracy/AUC; SVM gives the best cross-validated accuracy; Gaussian Naive Bayes has the highest test ROC-AUC. The clinical features are close to linearly separable after preprocessing, so the extra complexity of a forest does not buy accuracy on this dataset.
  6. Tuning was applied honestly. Grid search improved the cross-validated F1 of Random Forest (0.8708 → 0.8766) and Logistic Regression (0.8671 → 0.8685), but the small changes did not carry over to the 184-patient test split. The differences are within the fold-to-fold standard deviation (≈ 0.03–0.05), so no model is significantly better than the top group.

Which model performed best? On the held-out test set, Logistic Regression is best on accuracy (0.8859), F1 (0.8986) and recall (0.9118), with the second-best AUC (0.9323, behind 0.9430 for Gaussian Naive Bayes). Under 5-fold cross-validation, SVM is slightly ahead (0.8584 vs 0.8515), but by less than one standard deviation. We therefore select Logistic Regression as the final model: it has the best test performance, the most stable CV folds, and the most interpretable coefficients for a clinical audience. SVM is a very close alternative when non-linear decision boundaries are preferred.

Why Logistic Regression wins. After median imputation, one-hot encoding and standardisation, the clinical measurements have a strong, largely additive relationship with the log-odds of heart disease. L2 regularisation controls overfitting on the 734 training rows, and the model makes efficient use of the available signal without the variance of a single tree. Random Forest and SVM capture non-linearities but do not improve on this split; their similar AUC confirms that the signal is largely captured by the simpler model.

14. Limitations¶

  • Moderate sample size (918 patients) from five cohorts; the model may not transfer to other hospitals, populations or measurement protocols without external validation.
  • No true NaN values but many invalid zeros in Cholesterol (172) and RestingBP (1); median imputation may bias the cholesterol relationship, and the missingness is not random (152/172 zero cholesterol records belong to the disease group).
  • Single 80/20 test split for headline metrics; with only 184 test patients, confidence intervals are wide even though 5-fold cross-validation was also reported.
  • Limited hyperparameter search (48 forest configurations, 5 C values, not SVM/KNN grids in the final notebook); a wider randomized or Bayesian search could find better settings.
  • Tuning did not improve test performance, illustrating the risk of selecting hyperparameters on a small, noisy test set; nested cross-validation would give a cleaner estimate.
  • No probability calibration, so predicted probabilities should not be treated as exact risk.
  • No cost-sensitive threshold optimisation; in real screening, the threshold should be chosen based on the relative cost of false negatives and false positives.
  • Self-reported/retrospective labels and possible selection bias in the source cohorts.
  • The dataset does not include many modern risk factors (smoking, BMI, diabetes duration, medication, family history), which limits achievable performance.

15. Future Work¶

  • Try XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost, plus stacking/ensembling.
  • Add clinical feature engineering: heart-rate reserve, age-adjusted MaxHR, cholesterol ratio, interaction terms between ST_Slope and ExerciseAngina.
  • Use nested cross-validation for unbiased performance estimation with tuning.
  • Apply probability calibration (Platt/isotonic), cost-sensitive learning and threshold optimisation for screening.
  • Use SHAP values for consistent local explanations and clinician-facing reports.
  • Validate externally on another heart-disease cohort.
  • Deploy the saved pipeline with a small FastAPI/Flask service or dashboard.
